title: Effects of light transitions on measures of alertness, arousal and comfort
research_question: How do subjective experiences and objective measures of vigilance, arousal and thermoregulation develop over time after an acute light transition?

participants.description: Thirty-eight healthy subjects (19 female; Mage = 24, SDage = 2.9; range = 20-31 years old) completed all four conditions. Exclusions included extreme chronotype (Midsleep < 3.8 or > 6.6), pregnancy, medication other than the contraceptive pill, hypertension or cardiovascular diseases, and intercontinental travelling over the past three months.
participants.recruitment: recruited via the J.F. Schouten School for User-System Interaction Research database and screened through an eligibility questionnaire

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Participants were exposed to two strongly contrasting light settings: Warm, Dim (WD) light (CCT 2708 K, 97 lux on eye, 37 melanopic lux) and Cool, Bright (CB) light (CCT 5854 K, 1021 lux on eye, 855 melanopic lux). Four conditions were created: 1) Constant WD, 2) WD to CB transition, 3) Constant CB, 4) CB to WD transition. Each session lasted 90 minutes, with a 45-minute baseline (Phase I) and a 45-minute experimental phase (Phase II).

Averaged from visual comfort (illuminance) and visual comfort (color temperature)
Combined from Lively, Drowsy, Sleepy, Awake 5-point scales
iButton (DS1925) data-loggers (average of 14 ISO-defined body sites)

mechanisms: complex interplay of underlying physiological and psychological processes
image forming (IF) pathway of light (rapid onset, adaptation)
non-image forming (NIF) pathway of light (slower onset, persistence)
bias through anchoring of the response range (for antecedent effects on visual sensation)
relative nature of our perceptual system (for antecedent effects on visual sensation)
melatonin production (for physiological responses to light in evening/dark adaptation)
continued activating effect of prior light exposure (for DPG)
moderators: time of day (suggested for future research)
implementation_implications: Abrupt transitions in lighting can be used to alter subjective experiences in the built environment.
Light transitions towards cool, bright light are generally alerting and activating, but not necessarily comfortable.
Dynamic lighting can provide a mental boost or a calming experience at low cost.
When designing dynamic lighting, consider both the target light setting and the antecedent light setting, as the direction of transition matters.
Abrupt changes in light can alter the perception of the thermal environment.
Knowledge of response dynamics is required to design effective dynamic lighting scenarios for office environments.

tables.description: Participant descriptors including Body Mass Index, Midsleep (MSFsc), PSQI score, General Health (SF-36), Light Sensitivity (Eye Problems, Headache, Sunglasses), and Thermal Sensitivity.
a-opic irradiances of the Warm, Dim and Cool, Bright light settings, including S-cone-opic, M-cone-opic, L-cone-opic, Rhodopic, and Melanopic lux values.
Test statistics of main effect of transition for various dependent variables, comparing WD to CB vs. Constant WD, and CB to WD vs. Constant CB.

limitations: CCT and illuminance were manipulated simultaneously, preventing attribution of effects to either variable alone.
The study could not test whether time of day moderated effects due to group sizes and scheduling, despite its expected influence.
Only abrupt transitions were used; future research should investigate gradual transitions to see if negative results disappear and positive results remain.
The laboratory study lasted only 90 minutes; results need validation in longer experiments and field settings.
Physiological responses immediately after the transition were not quantified due to the PVT task starting 2-3 minutes into each measurement block.
